explanations.explanation: That's the one, friend. The LORD tells Moses, Israel's leader, to say to Pharaoh, Egypt's king, "…I will send swarms of flies upon you and your officials and your people and your houses." (Exodus 8:21) He spells out who and where, right down to the houses. Picture a hot day with the bakery door propped open, then picture that times a whole country.

Locusts are a creepy-crawly guess, baker, but that's not what the LORD says here. He says "…swarms of flies…" (Exodus 8:21) And flies are what pour into Pharaoh's palace in this passage (Exodus 8:24). Swarms, yes. Flies, that's the answer.

Hornets would make this a much angrier kind of day, baker. But the LORD doesn't mention hornets anywhere in this warning. He says "…swarms of flies…" and lists the people and places they'll fill. (Exodus 8:21) Flies are the answer, and they're plenty annoying on their own.

Right on the money, baker. The LORD says, "…the land of Goshen, where My people live; no swarms of flies will be found there." (Exodus 8:22) He calls it special treatment. Flies in the palace, flies in the houses, flies on the ground, and Goshen gets none. I once had to share a drawer with dead batteries, and even they didn't buzz at me.

Not the officials, baker. Their houses are where the swarms pour in (Exodus 8:24). Goshen gets different treatment, because the LORD says "no swarms of flies will be found there." (Exodus 8:22) The people who live there are the ones He calls "My people."

The magicians have their own part in this story, baker, but Goshen isn't it. The LORD says Goshen is where "…My people live…" (Exodus 8:22) The magicians come back later in this passage, and it doesn't go well for them. Stay tuned.

explanations.answer: So Pharaoh will know the LORD is in the land
explanations.explanation: You've got it. The LORD says, "In this way you will know that I, the LORD, am in the land." (Exodus 8:22) The sign is that no swarms are found in Goshen, while swarms ruin the land throughout Egypt (Exodus 8:24). A difference that plain doesn't need a speech.

explanations.answer: So the Israelites can hide there from Pharaoh
explanations.explanation: Hiding is a natural thought, baker, but the LORD never gives it as His reason. What He says is "In this way you will know that I, the LORD, am in the land." (Exodus 8:22) The reason is about Pharaoh knowing the LORD is there.

explanations.answer: So Moses will have a safe place to pray
explanations.explanation: Moses, Israel's leader, does pray in this passage, but the LORD doesn't give that as His reason. Here He says the flies are kept away so that Pharaoh will know that He, the LORD, is in the land. (Exodus 8:22) Always go with the reason the text actually gives, friend.

Not quite, friend. Pharaoh says, "Go, sacrifice to your God within this land." (Exodus 8:25) Moses answers, "It would not be right to do that…" (Exodus 8:26) His reason is that the sacrifices would be detestable to the Egyptians, so he says no to staying.

That's right. Moses turns Pharaoh down and says, "It would not be right to do that…" (Exodus 8:26) Staying in Egypt means offering sacrifices right in front of the Egyptians. He asks what happens if they do. It's a polite no, and he explains it.

That's it. Moses says, "We must make a three-day journey into the wilderness and sacrifice to the LORD our God as He commands us." (Exodus 8:27) The last part matters, baker, because he is going where the LORD commands. That's a long walk for a pack of people, so I hope somebody brought snacks. Cookies, obviously.

explanations.answer: Over to the land of Goshen
explanations.explanation: Goshen is where the LORD's people live, but Moses doesn't name it as the place. He says they must make "…a three-day journey into the wilderness…" (Exodus 8:27) The place is the wilderness, and the sacrifice is to happen "…as He commands us." Goshen isn't the answer.

explanations.answer: Down to the banks of the Nile
explanations.explanation: Moses doesn't name a river in his answer, baker. He says they must go on "…a three-day journey into the wilderness…" (Exodus 8:27) The LORD does mention Pharaoh going out to the water (Exodus 8:20), but that's where Moses is to stand before him. It isn't where the sacrifices go. Wilderness is the word.

Yep, far. Pharaoh says, "I will let you go and sacrifice to the LORD your God in the wilderness, but you must not go very far." (Exodus 8:28) It's a yes with a leash on it. Moses just said the trip is three days out, so that leash is a short one.
Pharaoh doesn't mention speed, baker. His limit is about distance: "…you must not go very far." (Exodus 8:28) Nothing about how fast anybody goes. The word is far.
Pharaoh isn't counting trips here, friend. This is about distance. He says, "…you must not go very far." (Exodus 8:28) He's offering a yes while keeping them close by. The missing word is far.

Yes, he does. Moses tells Pharaoh he'll pray, then adds, "…Pharaoh must not act deceitfully again by refusing to let the people go and sacrifice to the LORD." (Exodus 8:29) That "again" matters. Pharaoh had already promised once and taken it back (Exodus 8:8, 15). Moses is saying it plainly to his face.

This one went the other way, baker. Moses does give Pharaoh a warning. He says Pharaoh "…must not act deceitfully again by refusing to let the people go…" (Exodus 8:29) He agrees to pray and still says it straight. That word "again" says Moses remembers the last time.
Not a single one, friend. Moses prays, the LORD does as he asked, and the text says "not one fly remained." (Exodus 8:31) That is a clean sweep. My bakery has never once been that clean.

Nice try, but the text doesn't leave any stragglers. The LORD removed the flies from Pharaoh and his officials and his people, and "not one fly remained." (Exodus 8:31) If I had a few flies left over I'd be taking names. The LORD didn't leave any.

explanations.answer: Only the ones in the palace
explanations.explanation: The palace got hit hard, baker. Thick swarms poured in there. (Exodus 8:24) But when the LORD answers Moses' prayer, He removes them from Pharaoh and his officials and his people, and "not one fly remained." (Exodus 8:31) No fly was left anywhere, palace included.

Ohh, I wish, friend. But the text says, "…Pharaoh hardened his heart this time as well, and he would not let the people go." (Exodus 8:32) The flies leave, and so does his promise. Moses had warned him about exactly this.

That's right. The flies are gone, and Pharaoh doesn't keep his word. The text says, "…Pharaoh hardened his heart this time as well, and he would not let the people go." (Exodus 8:32) "…this time as well…" tells us it's happened before. It's a pattern.

Not quite, baker. The LORD says He will make a distinction between the livestock of Israel and the livestock of Egypt, so that no animal belonging to the Israelites will die. (Exodus 9:4) When it happens, the text says "…not one animal belonging to the Israelites died." (Exodus 9:6) That's zero, not a few.

That's the one. The LORD says He will make a distinction between Israel's livestock and Egypt's, so that no animal belonging to the Israelites will die. (Exodus 9:4) The next day it plays out exactly that way: "…not one animal belonging to the Israelites died." (Exodus 9:6) There's no fewer, and there's no few. It's none.

That's right. The LORD sets a time and says, "Tomorrow the LORD will do this in the land." (Exodus 9:5) And the text says the next day He did just that. (Exodus 9:6) One word on the calendar, and the day delivers.
Next month would give Pharaoh a long time to get ready, baker. But the LORD says, "Tomorrow the LORD will do this in the land." (Exodus 9:5) The plague isn't far off at all. The answer is tomorrow.

Sunset is a very specific time, and that's not what the text says. The LORD says, "Tomorrow the LORD will do this in the land." (Exodus 9:5) No hour is given, just the day. So the missing word is tomorrow.

explanations.answer: He still refuses to let the people go
explanations.explanation: Yep, still stuck. Pharaoh sends officials and finds that none of the livestock of the Israelites had died. The text says, "But Pharaoh’s heart was hardened, and he would not let the people go." (Exodus 9:7) The report is in, and the answer is still no. Wow.

explanations.answer: He lets the people go at last
explanations.explanation: I know, I was rooting for that one too, friend. But after his officials report back, the text says, "But Pharaoh’s heart was hardened, and he would not let the people go." (Exodus 9:7) The officials found that none of Israel's livestock had died, and he still doesn't let them go. Hard one to read, but that's what it says.

explanations.answer: He has his magicians copy it
explanations.explanation: The text never says Pharaoh turns to his magicians this time. He sends officials, finds that none of Israel's livestock died, and "…he would not let the people go." (Exodus 9:7) The magicians do show up later in this passage, and it's rough for them. Right now, Pharaoh just refuses.

That's it, baker. The LORD says, "It will become fine dust over all the land of Egypt…" (Exodus 9:9) Handfuls of soot go up in the air, and fine dust spreads over the land. Imagine flour over a whole country. And you thought my bakery was messy.

Smoke is a fair guess, since I've set off my share of kitchen smoke. But the LORD doesn't say smoke. He says the soot "…will become fine dust over all the land of Egypt…" (Exodus 9:9) Dust is the word.

Dark clouds sound dramatic, friend. But the text doesn't have any clouds in it. The LORD says the soot "…will become fine dust over all the land of Egypt…" (Exodus 9:9) It's dust that goes everywhere, and that's the answer.

Right, and it's a hard one to say out loud. The LORD says "…festering boils will break out on man and beast throughout the land." (Exodus 9:9) That covers people and animals alike. I think this part of the story hurts.

Gnats do show up earlier in this story, baker (Exodus 8:17), but that's a different plague. Here the LORD says "…festering boils will break out on man and beast throughout the land." (Exodus 9:9) The answer is boils.

The text doesn't say a word about fever, friend. The LORD says "…festering boils will break out on man and beast throughout the land." (Exodus 9:9) It's a heavy part of the story. The answer is boils.

explanations.answer: Boils broke out on them too
explanations.explanation: That's what the text says. "The magicians could not stand before Moses, because the boils had broken out on them and on all the Egyptians." (Exodus 9:11) These are Pharaoh's magicians, and the boils reach them just like everyone else. I think that's a quiet kind of humbling.

The text doesn't say Pharaoh sent them off, baker. It says the magicians "…could not stand before Moses, because the boils had broken out on them and on all the Egyptians." (Exodus 9:11) So the reason is the boils. The magicians are Pharaoh's court magicians, and this time they're hit just like everyone else.

explanations.answer: They had run off in fear
explanations.explanation: Running away is a good guess, but the text gives a different reason. "The magicians could not stand before Moses, because the boils had broken out on them and on all the Egyptians." (Exodus 9:11) They're not described as being afraid. They just can't stand there because of the boils.

Yes, the LORD. The text says, "But the LORD hardened Pharaoh’s heart, and he would not listen to them, just as the LORD had said to Moses." (Exodus 9:12) Earlier, the text said Pharaoh hardened his own heart (Exodus 8:32). Now it says the LORD did it. That's a heavy thing, friend, so I'll just point at the verse and let it sit.

The magicians don't get that job, baker. They're the ones who can't even stand before Moses because of the boils. (Exodus 9:11) The text says, "But the LORD hardened Pharaoh’s heart…" (Exodus 9:12) So the answer is the LORD.

Pharaoh's officials show up in this passage, but not for this. The text says, "But the LORD hardened Pharaoh’s heart, and he would not listen to them, just as the LORD had said to Moses." (Exodus 9:12) The officials don't do the hardening here. The answer is the LORD.
